en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 3. Exposition of the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka-sutta* (The Chapter on the Eight Corrupters)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Discourse on the Eightfold Corruption:
"Some indeed speak with corrupted minds,
and others likewise speak with truthful minds."
The Sage does not engage in arisen disputes;
therefore, for the Sage, there is no resentment anywhere.
Some indeed speak with evil minds—those sectarians who are evil-minded, corrupted in mind, hostile in mind, and antagonistic in mind.
With minds offended, with minds struck back, with minds provoked, with minds struck back again, they speak and revile the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with what is untrue—
some indeed speak thus with malicious minds.
Furthermore, it is those who, having faith in, relying upon, and being convinced by those sectarian teachers, speak with the thought that it is true, perceiving it as true;

who speak with the thought that it is real, perceiving it as real; who speak with the thought that it is so, perceiving it as so; who speak with the thought that it is according to fact, perceiving it as according to fact;
who speak with an unperverted mind, perceiving it without perversion—those who thus speak and reproach the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with what is untrue.
"Furthermore, they speak with truthful intent:
'The Sage does not engage in a dispute that has arisen.

That dispute has arisen, come into being, been produced, fully manifested, and appeared; it is a report from others, an abuse, and a reproach against the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, based on what is untrue."
"And the arisen dispute does not approach the sage. "The sage" means:
[the one who is silent].
"Mona" is said to be knowledge.
That which is wisdom, understanding, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—one who is endowed with that knowledge is a sage, one who has attained muna...
having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
Whoever enters into a dispute does so for two reasons:

either one enters into a dispute as an agent because of being an agent, or else, when being spoken to or criticized, one becomes angry, becomes resentful, becomes stubborn, and manifests anger, hatred, and ill-will.
Whoever enters into a dispute thinking "I am not the agent" enters into that dispute for these two reasons.
The sage does not enter into dispute for two reasons:

because he is a non-doer, the sage does not enter into dispute on account of his state as a non-doer; or else, when being spoken to or reviled, he does not become angry, does not give way to ill will, does not take a stand, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
"I am a non-doer"—for these two reasons the sage does not enter into dispute, does not approach it, does not grasp it, does not misapprehend it, and does not adhere to it.
And the arisen dispute does not approach the Sage.
Therefore, for the Sage, there is no stubbornness anywhere.
"Therefore" means: for that reason, on that account, by that cause, and with that as the basis, there is neither a struck-down mind nor the arising of stubbornness in the Sage.
There are no five mental barrennesses; there are no three barrennesses.

The barrenness of lust, the barrenness of hatred, and the barrenness of delusion do not exist, are not present, are not found, and are not obtainable; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again and are burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
"Anywhere" means anywhere at all, in anything whatsoever, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally.
"Therefore, for the Sage, there is no stubbornness anywhere.
Thus the Blessed One said:
"Indeed, some who are ill-minded speak..."
Furthermore, they speak with truthful minds;
yet the sage does not enter into any arisen dispute.
Therefore, for the sage, there is no obstruction anywhere.
For how could one overcome his own view when he is led by desire,
settled in his own preference,
and acting according to his own convictions?
For one should speak exactly as one knows;
for how could one conceal one's own view?
Thus, those sectarians, having killed the wanderer Sundarī, proclaimed dispraise of the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan.
“Thus we shall bring back gain, fame, honor, and respect,” they thought; holding such views, such inclinations, such preferences, such convictions,
such dispositions, and such intentions, they were unable to transcend their own views,
their own inclinations, their own preferences, their own convictions, their own dispositions, and their own intentions.
Or rather, it is he himself who has returned to his own position;
for how could one abandon one's own view? Or else, as for that proponent who says, "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false," he [abandons] his own view.
How could one pass over, transcend, surpass, or go beyond one's own preference, one's own inclination, one's own view, one's own disposition,
or one's own intention? For what reason?
That view of his was thus fully accepted, undertaken, grasped, adhered to, settled upon, and resolved upon. And so,
how could he ever abandon his own view?

“Is the world eternal? … Is the world finite? … Is the world infinite? … [and so forth] … “Is the world finite and infinite? … [and so forth] … “Does the Tathāgata exist after death? … Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? … Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? … Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? … [and so forth] … “Are the soul and the body the same? … Are the soul and the body different? … [and so forth] … “Does the Tathāgata exist after death? Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? … [and so forth] … “Is the world eternal? Is the world not eternal? Is the world both eternal and not eternal? Is the world neither eternal nor not eternal? … [and so forth] … “Is the world finite? Is the world infinite? Is the world both finite and infinite? Does the Tathāgata exist after death? Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? Does the Tathāgata both
"The soul is the same as the body" ...
"the soul is one thing and the body another" ...
"a Tathāgata exists after death" ...

“The Tathāgata does not exist after death… the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death… the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish,” whoever says this—
Speaking thus, how could he let go of, transcend, surpass, or pass beyond his own view, his own preference, his own inclination,
his own conviction, his own disposition, and his own intention? For what reason?
That view of his was thus fully accepted, undertaken, grasped, adhered to, settled upon, and resolved upon.
In this way too:
how indeed could one abandon one's own view?
"Led by desire, settled in preference. "Led by desire" means that one is led,
guided, carried away, and swept along by one's own view, one's own inclination, one's own preference, and one's own conviction—
just as one might be carried by an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, a chariot-vehicle, a cow-vehicle, a goat-vehicle, or a sheep-vehicle.
Just as one travels, is led out, is carried away, or is driven along by means of a cart, a carriage, or a chariot, so too one travels, is led out, is carried away,
or is driven along by means of one’s own view, one’s own inclination, one’s own preference, and one’s own conviction— one who is thus led by desire is called "one who follows desire."
"Established in one's own preference" means established, settled, attached, approached, clung to, and intent upon one's own view, one's own preference, and one's own conviction—
one who is led by desire and established in preference.
"Acting according to what one has oneself resolved."
He makes it complete; he makes it fulfilled; he makes it sublime; he makes it the foremost, the best, the most distinguished, the preeminent, the supreme, the excellent.

Thinking, "This Teacher is omniscient," he makes it complete; he makes it fulfilled; he makes it sublime; he makes it the foremost, the best, the most distinguished, the preeminent, the supreme, the excellent.
[Thinking,] "This Dhamma is well-expounded; this Saṅgha is practicing rightly; this view is auspicious; this is the right path..."
"This path is well-proclaimed, leading to liberation"— thus he makes it complete for himself, fulfills it, makes it sublime,
the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the preeminent, the highest, and the most excellent; he generates it, produces it, brings it forth, and fully manifests it.
Acting with full commitment:
"As one knows, so one should speak. Just as one would know, so one should speak, say, utter, explain, and declare:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Just as one would know, so one should speak, say, utter, explain, and declare.

“If one were to say, speak, declare, explain, illuminate, or express: ‘The world is eternal… [or] the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—one would speak according to how one knows.
Thus, one would speak according to how one knows.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“How indeed could one overcome his own view,
when he is led by desire and settled in his own preference?”
"Having performed them himself,
he should speak of them exactly as he knows them.
A person who [knows] his own virtuous practices...
One should not practice ignoble conduct toward others without being asked;
the wise call that ignoble conduct which one practices against oneself by one's own hand.
"Whatever person's virtuous observances...

Here, "whatever" means whoever—of whatever kind, as is appropriate, as is ordained, of whatever character, having reached whatever station, endowed with whatever qualities—be they a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a vaiśya, a śūdra, a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human.
Regarding "virtuous observances": there is that which is both virtue (*sīla*) and observance (*vata*), and there is that which is an observance but not virtue.
What is virtue and observance?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
Whatever therein is restraint, self-control, and non-transgression—this is virtue.
That which is an undertaking is a vow.
In the sense of restraint it is virtue;
in the sense of undertaking it is a vow.
This is called both virtue and observance.
What is observance that is not virtue?
The eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas).

The forest-dweller’s practice, the alms-food-eater’s practice, the rag-robe-wearer’s practice, the triple-robe-wearer’s practice, the house-to-house-seeker’s practice, the one-after-another-meal-eater’s practice, the sitter’s practice, and the any-bed-user’s practice—
this is called a vow (*vata*), not virtue (*sīla*).
The undertaking of energy is also called a vow, not virtue.
“Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in the body.
That which is to be attained by manly strength, manly power, manly energy, and manly exertion—that I shall not fail to reach; my energy shall not falter”—thus he exerts his mind and strives.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow, not virtue.
"I shall neither eat nor drink," [he thinks].
I shall not emerge from the monastery,
nor shall I cast down my gaze as long as the arrow of craving has not been extracted.
One exerts the mind and strives.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow (vata), not virtue (sīla).
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging"—this is a vow, not virtue.
He exerts and strives his mind.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow (*vata*), not virtue (*sīla*).
"I shall not rise from this seat until..."
I shall descend from the walkway;
I shall depart from the monastery;
I shall depart from the half-roofed hut.
I shall emerge from the palace,
I shall emerge from the upper terrace,
I shall emerge from the cave.
I shall emerge from the cave,
I shall emerge from the hut,
I shall emerge from the gabled house.
I shall go out from the watchtower;
I shall go out from the upper story;
I shall go out from the high rampart.
"I shall depart from the assembly hall,
I shall depart from the pavilion,
I shall depart from the foot of the tree, until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging."
One exerts and strives the mind.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a *vata* (vow), not *sīla* (virtue). [Thinking:
"In this very morning session, I shall bring forth the noble Dhamma, I shall gather it together, I shall attain it, I shall touch it, I shall realize it"—this is called a *vata*, not *sīla*.
One exerts and strives the mind.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a *vata* (vow), not *sīla* (virtue).
“At this very time of midday...”
In the evening,
before the meal,
or after the meal.
the first watch,
the middle watch,
and the last watch;
In the dark fortnight, in the bright fortnight, and during the rainy season.
In winter,
in summer,
and in the first stage of life,
“During the middle stage of life and the final stage of life, I will bring forth the noble Dhamma, I will gather it, I will attain it, I will touch it, and I will realize it”—
thus he exerts his mind and strives.
Even such an undertaking of energy is called a *vata* (vow), not *sīla* (virtue). "A person" (*jantu*) means a being,
a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a human, a mortal—
one who, as a person, possesses his own virtues and vows.
"One brings misfortune to others without being asked.
"To others" means to other khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans.
"Without being asked" means unasked, unrequested, uninvited, unsolicited, and unpleased.
"Pāva" means he proclaims his own virtue, or vow, or both virtue and vow.

Or else, he [proclaims it] by way of birth, clan, lineage, beauty of complexion, wealth, or learning, thinking: "I am endowed with virtue," or "endowed with vows," or "endowed with both virtue and vows."
Whether by means of a craft, a profession, a branch of knowledge, learning, or eloquence; or by some other basis such as:

"He has gone forth from a high-ranking family," or "He has gone forth from a great family," or "He has gone forth from a family of great wealth," or "He has gone forth from a family of magnificent wealth";
or "He is well-known and famous among householders and renunciants," or "He is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
Whether as a master of the Suttas, or a bearer of the Vinaya, or an expounder of the Dhamma, or a forest-dweller, or an alms-collector,
or a wearer of rag-robes, or one who possesses only three robes, or a house-to-house seeker of alms, or one who eats only from a single bowl, or a sitter,
or one who accepts whatever seat is offered—
Whether as one who has attained the first jhāna, or as one who has attained the second jhāna, or as one who has attained the third jhāna,
or as one who has attained the fourth jhāna, or as one who has attained the base of infinite space,
or as one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, or as one who has attained the base of nothingness;
To proclaim, speak, declare, illuminate, or express that one has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without being asked by others—
this they call an ignoble state among the skilled.
"Skilled" refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,

skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, skilled in the path, skilled in the fruits,
and skilled in Nibbāna; these skilled ones spoke thus:—
“This is the nature of the ignoble; this is not the nature of the noble.
This is the nature of fools; this is not the nature of the wise.
This is the nature of the unvirtuous; this is not the nature of the virtuous.”
"They speak thus, they talk thus, they say thus, they illuminate thus, they express themselves thus"—
the wise call that the ignoble state (anariyadhamma),
which one brings upon oneself by one's own doing.
"Ātumā" is called "self.
One proclaims oneself— that is, one declares oneself—
"I am endowed with virtue," or "endowed with vows," or "endowed with both virtue and vows."
Whether by birth, or clan, or family lineage, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation,
or field of craft, or branch of science, or learning, or eloquence, or by some other basis— thinking,

"He has gone forth from a high family," or "He has gone forth from a great family," or "He has gone forth from a family of great wealth," or "He has gone forth from a family of magnificent wealth," or "He is well-known and famous among both householders and those who have gone forth."
"Whether one thinks: 'I am a recipient of robes, almsfood,

lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,' or 'I am a master of the Suttantas,' or 'a bearer of the Vinaya,' or 'an expounder of the Dhamma,' or 'a forest-dweller,' or 'an alms-food eater,' or 'a wearer of rag-robes,' or 'one who possesses only three robes,' or 'one who goes on a continuous alms-round,' or 'one who eats only after the meal has been prepared,' or 'one who remains in the sitting posture.'"
Or one who is content with whatever seat is provided;
or one who is an attainer of the first jhāna, or an attainer of the second jhāna, or an attainer of the third jhāna,
or an attainer of the fourth jhāna, or an attainer of the attainment of the base of infinite space.

Or, one who proclaims, speaks, declares, elucidates, and expresses that "I am an attainer of the base of infinite space," or "I am an attainer of the base of infinite consciousness," or "I am an attainer of the base of nothingness," or "I am an attainer of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—
this is one who proclaims himself by his own accord.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The person who, without being asked,
proclaims his own virtuous practices to others;”
The wise call that ignoble state which one brings upon oneself by one's own doing;
yet the peaceful bhikkhu has attained complete extinction within himself.
One who does not boast regarding their virtues destroys [the defilements];
the wise call that the noble dhamma,
for which there is no conceit anywhere in the world.
And a bhikkhu is "peaceful" because he is fully extinguished.
He is peaceful because passion has been stilled;
he is peaceful because hatred has been stilled.
One is peaceful through the subsiding of delusion;
[one is peaceful] through the subsiding of anger… through the subsiding of resentment…
of hypocrisy … of spite … of envy …
Of stinginess ...
of deceit ...
of craftiness ...
of arrogance… of contentiousness… of conceit…
of overweening pride … of intoxication … of negligence …
Of all defilements … of all misconduct … of all fevers …
Because all fevers have been calmed, stilled, tranquilized, extinguished, quenched, removed, and subsided;

because all torments... because all unwholesome formations have been calmed, stilled, tranquilized, extinguished, quenched, removed, and subsided—one is called "peaceful, calmed, tranquilized, quenched, and subsided."
The virtuous ones.
A "bhikkhu" is so called because he has broken seven things:
personality-belief is broken, doubt is broken, adherence to rules and observances is broken, lust is broken, hatred is broken, delusion is broken, and conceit is broken.
“Evil, unwholesome states— corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death— are shattered within him.
“By the path made by oneself,” said the Blessed One to Sabhiya, “one goes to the destination according to one’s own deeds.”
Having attained final Nibbāna, having crossed over doubt,
and having abandoned both non-existence and existence,
that bhikkhu has lived the holy life and is one for whom rebirth is exhausted.
And a bhikkhu is "one who has attained peace" because he has extinguished lust, because he has extinguished hatred, because he has extinguished delusion, because he has extinguished anger...
resentment... contempt...
[and so forth].
of malice … of envy … of avarice …
Of deceit … of guile … of obstinacy …
of aggression … of conceit … of arrogance …
Of intoxication … of negligence … of all defilements …
Of all misconducts … of all fevers … of all burning agonies …
Because all fevers have been extinguished and because all unwholesome volitional formations have been quenched,
he is a bhikkhu at peace, one whose self is fully quenched.
"Itihanti sīlesu akatthamāno":

*Iti* is the conjunction of words, the association of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words; this is what "iti" means. "Hanti" means he destroys. "Sīlesu" means in the precepts. "Akatthamāno" means not being boastful. Thus: "Itihanti sīlesu akatthamāno."
"Not boasting about virtues":
here, a certain person is a boaster, a great boaster;
he boasts and greatly boasts.
“I am endowed with virtue,” or “I am endowed with observances,” or “I am endowed with both virtue and observances,” or on account of birth,
clan, lineage, or the beauty of one’s complexion …pe… or “I am an attainer of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception”— thus he boasts and exults.
Thus he does not boast, nor does he disparage others.
Being free from boasting, abstaining from it, refraining from it, having emerged from it, having escaped it, and being fully liberated, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—
thus, "so it is," he does not boast regarding his virtues.
"The skilled ones speak of that true Dhamma. Here,
"the skilled ones" refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,
skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, and skilled in the path.
Skilled in the fruit and skilled in Nibbāna, those who are skilled speak thus:
"This is the Dhamma of the noble ones; this is not the Dhamma of the ignoble.
This is the Dhamma of the wise; this is not the Dhamma of the foolish."
“This is the Dhamma of true persons; this is not the Dhamma of untrue persons.
Thus they speak, thus they discourse, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, thus they express themselves regarding the noble ones—they, being skilled, speak of that noble Dhamma.
"Of whom there is no swelling anywhere in the world.
"Of whom" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Swelling" refers to the seven swellings (*ussada*).
The inflation of lust, the inflation of hatred, the inflation of delusion, the inflation of conceit, the inflation of views, the inflation of defilements, and the inflation of kamma.

For one in whom these inflations do not exist, are not present, are not found, and are not obtained—having been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—wherein?
"Wherein" means anywhere, in anything, in some place: either internally, or externally, or both internally and externally.
"In the world"— that is, in the world of the lower realms, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases—
he has no conceit anywhere in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The bhikkhu who is holy, whose self is extinguished,
and who does not boast about his virtues—
him the skillful call the noble Dhamma.”
“For whom there is no conceit anywhere in the world.
For one whose fabricated, conditioned phenomena have been laid aside,
who stands before them, yet remains unpurified;
One who sees a benefit in what belongs to oneself is dependent on that which is unstable and a peace attained through conditions; for him,
all phenomena are merely fashioned and conditioned.
"Formations" (pakappanā) refers to two kinds of formations:
the formation of craving and the formation of views...
[as follows] ...this is the formation of craving... [as follows] ...
This is the formulation of views.
"Conditioned" means conditioned, constructed, and put together— thus it is called "conditioned."
Alternatively, "conditioned" means: impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
"Of whom" refers to the one who holds wrong views.
"Phenomena" (dhammā) are said to be the sixty-two types of views—
for whom phenomena have been fashioned and conditioned,
who are preceded by them, and who remain unpurified.
"Placed before" refers to two kinds of precedence:
the precedence of craving and the precedence of views...
[as above] ...this is the precedence of craving... [as above] ...
This is one who prioritizes views.
For him, the prioritization of craving is not abandoned, and the prioritization of views is not relinquished.
Because he has not abandoned the prioritization of craving and has not relinquished the prioritization of views, he [pursues] craving...
Or, having placed either craving or views before oneself, one proceeds with craving as the banner, craving as the standard, and craving as the overlord;
or with views as the banner, views as the standard, and views as the overlord; one proceeds surrounded by either craving or views—thus they are "placed before."
"They exist" means they are present, found, there, and obtainable.
"Not bright" means not clear, not pure, impure, defiled, and subject to defilement—
these are the non-bright ones who stand before one.
"Whatever benefit he sees in himself":
"in himself" means in what pertains to the self.
"Self" refers to a speculative view.
One sees two benefits in one’s own view:
the benefit pertaining to the present life and the benefit pertaining to future lives.
What is the benefit of the view pertaining to the present life?
Whatever view the teacher holds, his disciples hold that same view.
The disciples honor, revere, respect, worship, and pay homage to the teacher who holds that view.
And because of this, they receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This is the benefit pertaining to the present life from this view.
What is the benefit pertaining to future lives from this view?
This view is sufficient for the state of a *nāga*, or a *supaṇṇa*, or a *yakkha*, or an *asura*, or a *gandhabba*, or a Great King, or Indra, or Brahmā, or a deva.
“This view is for the sake of purification, cleansing, complete purification; for liberation, emancipation, and complete emancipation.
By means of this view, they are purified, cleansed, completely purified; they are liberated, emancipated, and completely emancipated.
‘By means of this view I shall be purified, cleansed, and completely purified; I shall be liberated, emancipated, and completely emancipated’—thus one becomes expectant of a future fruit.”
This is the future benefit of one’s own view.
One sees, beholds, looks upon, contemplates, and examines these two benefits in one’s own view;
thus, it is "the benefit that one sees in oneself."
"Dependent on that, it is a peace based on the unstable.
There are three kinds of peace:
absolute peace, peace by way of substitution, and conventional peace.
What is absolute peace?
Absolute peace is called the deathless Nibbāna.
It is that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
This is ultimate peace.
What is peace by way of its factors?
For one who has attained the first jhāna, the hindrances are stilled.
For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought are stilled;
for one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture is stilled;
for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, pleasure and pain are stilled.
For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity have become stilled;
for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has become stilled;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has become stilled.
For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has subsided.
This is peace by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgasanti*).
What is conventional peace (*sammutisanti*)?
The sixty-two types of speculative views are called "peace through conventional designation" (*sammuti-santi*).
Furthermore, in this context, "peace" (*santi*) is intended to mean conventional peace.
That which relies upon it is "peace that is unstable and dependent."
Whether it be a peace that is disturbed, a peace that is agitated, a peace that is shaken, a peace that is tossed about, a peace that is moved, a peace that is struck,
a peace that is fashioned, or a peace that is contrived— being impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction,

subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation; one who relies on such peace, who is not detached from it, who clings to it, who has approached it, who is obsessed with it, and who is intent upon it— [is said to be "one who relies on peace"].
He relies on that unstable peace which is dependently arisen.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whose states are fashioned and conditioned...”
Those who are placed first are not truly pure;
one who sees a benefit in what belongs to oneself is dependent on a peace that relies on the unstable.
For one who has not transcended the settling upon views,
having grasped what is determined among phenomena;
therefore, a person regarding those settled views—
"He rejects and grasps at phenomena; for he has not transcended his adherence to views.
"Adherence to views" refers to the dogmatic insistence and misapprehension that thinks, "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain"—this is the settling into views.
“Is the world eternal… is the world finite… is the world infinite…”
"The soul is the same as the body" ...
"the soul is one thing and the body another" ...
"a Tathāgata exists after death" ...
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death;
this alone is the truth, all else is foolish,” such dogmatic adherence and clinging to views is called *diṭṭhinivesana* (the settling on views).

"Indeed, the settling on views is not easily overcome": indeed, the settling on views is not easily overcome; it is difficult to overcome, hard to cross over, hard to traverse, hard to transcend, and hard to turn back from—thus, "indeed, the settling on views is not easily overcome.
"Having discerned among phenomena, one has grasped [the truth]."
"In phenomena" means among the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"Having determined" means having determined, having decided, having investigated, having scrutinized, having weighed, having deliberated, having analyzed, and having made manifest.
"Grasped" means a seizing within fixed positions: seizing as a pit, seizing as a hole, seizing as a peak, seizing as a section, seizing as a heap, and seizing as a collection.
"This is true, real, such, factual, as it is, and unerring"—thus it is grasped, adhered to, settled upon, clung to, and resolved upon.
This is what is called "the firm conviction held among phenomena.
Therefore, it is said: "Therefore, a person [is bound] to those dwellings."
Therefore, for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, by that source.
"A person" (*nara*) means a being, a person, a youth, a man, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a human, a son of Manu.
"In those abodes" means in those abodes of views.
"Therefore, a person, amidst those dwellings,
lets go and takes up the Dhamma.
"Lets go" means he lets go for two reasons:
Either he discards it to cut off another, or he discards it because he is unable to accomplish it.
How does he discard it to cut off another?
Another cuts it off.
Thus the Teacher is not omniscient,
the Dhamma is not well-expounded,
and the Saṅgha is not practicing rightly.
The view is not auspicious,
the practice is not well-proclaimed,
the path does not lead to liberation; herein there is no purity, nor purification, nor complete purity, nor freedom, nor liberation.
Or liberation; herein there is no cleansing, no purifying, no complete purification, no being freed, no being liberated, no complete liberation;
they are inferior, base, low, wretched, fourfold, and limited—in this way the other cuts off [the inquiry].
Being thus cut off, he rejects the Teacher, rejects the proclamation of the Dhamma, rejects the Saṅgha, rejects the view, rejects the practice, and rejects the path.
This is how he rejects by means of cutting others off.
How does he reject by failing to achieve?
Failing to fulfill virtue, one abandons virtue; failing to fulfill the vow, one abandons the vow; failing to fulfill both virtue and the vow, one abandons both virtue and the vow.
Thus, failing to fulfill them, one abandons them.
And one takes up a doctrine.
One takes up the Teacher, one takes up the teaching of the Dhamma, one takes up the community, one takes up a view, one takes up the practice, one takes up the path;
one misapprehends it and adheres to it—thus one rejects and yet grasps at the Dhamma.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Indeed, those settled in views do not transcend them;
they have grasped what they have decided upon among phenomena.
Therefore, a person, amidst those very settlements, ... [remains entangled].”
"He casts away and takes up phenomena.
For the one who has shaken off defilements, there is no preconceived view anywhere in the world regarding various states of existence.
Having abandoned both illusion and conceit,
the one who is cleansed— by what means could he go?
For that cleansed one has no fabricated view anywhere in the world regarding existence after existence.
He cleanses.
"Cleansing" (dhonā) is said to be wisdom (paññā)—
that which is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, close discernment, and precise discernment.
Wisdom, skill, proficiency, discernment, reflection, investigation, vast intelligence, guidance, insight, clear comprehension,

the goad, understanding, the faculty of understanding, the power of understanding, the sword of understanding, the palace of understanding, the light of understanding, the radiance of understanding, the lamp of understanding,
the jewel of understanding, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
For what reason is wisdom called "shaken off"?
Because by means of that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and purified;
verbal misconduct...
Mental misconduct has been shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and completely cleansed;
lust has been shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and completely cleansed;
hatred...
Delusion … anger … resentment …
Deceit is shaken off,
washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and completely purified;
envy is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and completely purified.
Avarice is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and completely cleansed;
deceit is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and completely cleansed;
guile is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and completely cleansed.
Stiffness is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified; likewise with aggression, pride, and so forth.
Excessive pride … intoxication … negligence are shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and purified.
All defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
For that reason, wisdom is called "the shaker" (*dhona*).
Alternatively, by means of right view, wrong view has been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
By right intention, wrong intention is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed,
and purified; by right speech, wrong speech is shaken off,
washed away … [and so on] … by right action, wrong action is shaken off … [and so on].
By right livelihood, wrong livelihood is shaken off;
by right effort, wrong effort is shaken off;
by right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is shaken off.
By right concentration, wrong concentration is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified; by right knowledge,
wrong knowledge is shaken off … by right liberation,
wrong liberation is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.

Alternatively, by means of the noble eightfold path, all defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken out, washed away, cleansed, and thoroughly purified.
The Arahant is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, furnished with, fully furnished with, and equipped with these qualities that are to be shaken out;
therefore, the Arahant is "one who has shaken off" (dhona).
Thus, one whose passion is shaken off, whose evil is shaken off, whose defilements are shaken off, and whose fever is shaken off is called "shaken off" (dhona).
"Anywhere" (kuhiñci) means anywhere at all— in anything whatsoever, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally.
"In the world" means in the world of the states of misery …pe… in the world of the sense bases.
"Constructed" refers to two kinds of construction:
the construction of craving and the construction of views …pe…
This is the fabrication of craving... [and so on] ...this is the fabrication of views.

"In various states of existence" means in various states of existence: in the state of kamma, in renewed existence, in the state of sensual desire; in the state of kamma, in the state of sensual desire, in renewed existence.

In the form existence, in the kamma existence, in the form existence, in renewed existence, in the formless existence, in the kamma existence, in the formless existence, in renewed existence—again and again in existence, again and again in destiny, again and again in rebirth, again and again in rebirth-linking, again and again in the manifestation of a personal identity.
For the one who is cleansed (*dhona*), there is no fabricated view anywhere in the world regarding various states of existence; thus, for the cleansed one, nowhere...
In the world, regarding various states of existence, whatever view has been fashioned, intended, conditioned, and established—that does not exist, is not present, is not found, and is not obtained;
it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided; it is incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
For the one who is cleansed, there is no fashioned view anywhere in the world concerning various states of existence.
"Having abandoned deceit and conceit, he is a cleanser.
Deceit is said to be a deceptive course of conduct.
Here, someone having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, forms an evil wish for the sake of concealing it: [namely,] "May people think of me thus..."
“He wishes, ‘May they not know me’; he intends, ‘May they not know me’; he speaks the words, ‘May they not know me’; he exerts himself with the body, ‘May they not know me.

Whatever such deception, deceitfulness, overstepping, cheating, crookedness, concealment, hiding, covering up, shielding, concealing, non-disclosure, non-revelation, suppression, and performance of evil deeds—this is called *māyā*.
As for *māna*, it is of one kind: pride.”
It is the inflation of the mind.
Pride is twofold:
pride consisting in self-exaltation and pride consisting in the disparagement of others.
Pride is threefold:
the pride of thinking “I am superior,” the pride of thinking “I am equal,” and the pride of thinking “I am inferior.
Pride is fourfold:
One generates conceit through gain; one generates conceit through fame; one generates conceit through praise; one generates conceit through pleasure. Conceit is fivefold:
one generates conceit thinking, "I am a possessor of agreeable forms"; one generates conceit thinking, "I am a possessor of agreeable sounds" ... [and so on for smells, tastes, and tangibles].
...of odors ...
of tastes ...
of tangibles," he generates conceit.
Pride in six ways:
one generates pride through the possession of the eye, through the possession of the ear, through the possession of the nose... [and so forth].
One generates conceit on account of excellence of the tongue … excellence of the body … excellence of the mind.
Pride is sevenfold:
pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, inferiority pride, superiority pride, the "I am" pride, and false pride.
Pride is eightfold:
Through gain one generates conceit; through loss one generates self-contempt; through fame one generates conceit; through disrepute one generates self-contempt;
through praise one generates conceit; through blame one generates self-contempt; through pleasure one generates conceit; through pain one generates self-contempt. This is ninefold conceit.
The conceit "I am superior" in one who is superior; the conceit "I am equal" in one who is superior; the conceit "I am inferior" in one who is superior;
the conceit "I am superior" in one who is equal; the conceit "I am equal" in one who is equal;

the conceit "I am inferior" in one who is equal; the conceit "I am superior" in one who is inferior; the conceit "I am equal" in one who is inferior; and the conceit "I am inferior" in one who is inferior.
Pride is tenfold:
here someone generates pride on account of birth, or clan, or lineage, or beauty of complexion,
or wealth, or learning, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science, or erudition.
Or by way of eloquence, or by way of some other basis whatsoever.
Whatever is such conceit, the act of conceiving, the state of conceiving, loftiness, haughtiness, a banner, grasping, the desire for a flag of the mind—
this is called conceit (*māna*).
"Having abandoned deceit and conceit, he is cleansed.
"Cleansed" means: having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and caused to cease existence, both deceit and conceit—he is cleansed, having abandoned deceit and conceit.
“By what means would he go, being without attachment?
There are two kinds of attachment:
attachment through craving and attachment through views... [etc.]...
This is the resort of craving... [and so on] ...this is the resort of views.
His resort of craving has been abandoned; his resort of views has been relinquished.
Because of the abandoning of the attachment to craving and the relinquishing of the attachment to views, by what passion would a person who is free from attachments go?
By what hatred would they go? By what delusion would they go? By what conceit would they go? By what view would they go?
By what restlessness would they go? By what doubt would they go? By what...?
One might proceed with underlying tendencies—
whether as one who is lustful, or hateful, or deluded, or bound, or obsessed, or distracted, or fallen into the undesirable, or become firmly rooted.
Those volitional formations have been abandoned.

With the abandoning of volitional formations, by what means could one go to any destination—whether as a denizen of hell, or as a being of the animal womb, or as a being in the realm of hungry ghosts, or as a human, or as a deva; whether possessing form or formless, percipient or non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient?
There is no cause, there is no condition, there is no reason by which one could go.
By what means could he go, for he is without support?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"For the one who is cleansed, there is nothing anywhere in the world..."
Having abandoned views conceived regarding various states of existence,
and having cast off illusion and conceit,
being free from clinging— by what means could he go anywhere?
For one who employs means among phenomena enters into dispute;
how could one who is without means engage in speech?
For him, there is neither self nor non-self.
He has here cast off every view;
for they say that one who is attached to phenomena becomes involved in disputes.
There are two kinds of attachment: [attachment to views and attachment to craving].
The one who relies on craving and the one who relies on views ... [as before] ...
this is the one who relies on craving ... [as before] ... this is the one who relies on views.
His approach through craving is not abandoned, and his approach through views is not relinquished.
Because his approach through craving is not abandoned and his approach through views is not relinquished, he enters into disputes regarding phenomena—
claiming one is "lustful," or "hateful," or "deluded," or "bound," or "misapprehending," or "wavering," or "fallen into the undesirable," or "become obstinate."
Those volitional formations have not been abandoned.
Because volitional formations have not been abandoned, one enters into dispute regarding rebirth:
"One is a denizen of hell," or "one is born in the animal realm," or "one is in the sphere of hungry ghosts," or "one is a human," or "one is a deva," or "one is possessed of form."

Or whether one enters into, approaches, grasps, clings to, and adheres to a doctrine such as "I am material" or "I am immaterial," or "I am percipient" or "I am non-percipient," or "I am neither percipient nor non-percipient"—
for one who is intent upon phenomena enters into such a doctrine.
"How could one speak of that which is without means?
There are two kinds of means:
the means of craving and the means of views... [and so on].
This is the resort to craving... [and so on] ...this is the resort to views.
For him, the resort to craving has been abandoned, and the resort to views has been relinquished.

Because of the abandoning of the approach of craving and the relinquishing of the approach of views, by what lust would one speak of a person who is without approach? By what hatred? By what delusion? By what conceit? By what view?
By what restlessness? By what doubt? By what underlying tendencies would one speak of him?
Whether as "lustful," or "hateful," or "deluded," or "bound," or "clinging," or "distracted," or "gone to the undesirable," or "become firm"—
these volitional formations have been abandoned.
Because volitional formations have been abandoned, by what means could one speak of destinations?
Whether it be "one bound for hell" ...
or "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—
there is no cause, no condition, no reason by which one might say, speak, utter, illuminate, or express [such things].
How could one who does not employ means speak?
For him there is neither self nor non-self; thus, there is no view of a self.
"Niratta" means there is no annihilationist view;
"atta" means there is nothing grasped;
"niratta" means there is nothing to be relinquished.
For whom there is grasping, for him there is that which must be released;
for whom there is that which must be released, for him there is grasping.
The Arahant has transcended both grasping and releasing, having passed beyond the fluctuation of intellect.
Having completed his residence [in the training], having practiced the conduct, having traversed the path and reached the destination, he has ended the cycle of birth and death;
for him there is no further becoming—thus, for him there is neither self nor non-self.

He has washed away every view right here: the sixty-two types of speculative views have been abandoned by him, cut off, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Thus, right here he washed away, shook off, blew away, wiped out, abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and led to non-existence all speculative views—
“He washed away every view right here.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one who employs means among phenomena enters into dispute;
how could one who is without means engage in talk?
For him there is neither self nor non-self.”
"He has here and now shaken off every view.
This concludes the third exposition, the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa*.
